claims.text: Spin-polarized DFT can be used to identify ferromagnetic ground states in complex alloys.
High-entropy alloys are disordered, multi-principal-element alloys.
The candidate alloy should be modeled in its equilibrium, minimum-energy crystalline state.
Spin-polarized DFT should be used to compute total energies for non-magnetic, ferromagnetic, and antiferromagnetic configurations.
The calculations represent zero- or low-temperature conditions.
Relaxed structural models can mimic the alloy's microstructure.
Exchange-correlation interactions drive the alignment of local magnetic moments and associated electronic structure.
Spin-polarized DFT includes energetic contributions associated with electron-spin alignment.
Comparing total energies of alternative magnetic configurations can determine which magnetic configuration is the ground state.
A ferromagnetic configuration with the lowest calculated total energy indicates a ferromagnetic ground state.
The candidate alloy's ferromagnetic configuration will have lower total energy than its non-magnetic or other magnetic configurations.
Non-magnetic and antiferromagnetic total energies provide baselines for comparison with the ferromagnetic configuration.
The prediction applies under idealized conditions such as perfect crystallinity and zero temperature.
Idealized calculations may not directly capture finite-temperature effects or structural disorder in real samples.
Thermal fluctuations and disorder can influence the calculated or observed magnetic behavior.
Spin-polarized DFT can indicate a ferromagnetic tendency, but quantitative predictions require further scrutiny.
SQUID magnetometry over a low-temperature range can measure the alloy's magnetic behavior.
Spontaneous magnetization and a defined Curie temperature are signatures that can support ferromagnetic behavior.
